title: MedRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Medical Agents via Clinically Aligned Self-Evolution
content: Medical agents increasingly combine general reasoning models with specialized clinical tools, yet their capabilities remain largely fixed by what clinicians and engineers design before deployment. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a different paradigm in which agents learn from their own failures and autonomously expand their capabilities, but directly applying RSI to medicine introduces fundamental safety challenges. We introduce MedRSI, the first recursive self-improvement framework for medicine, which continuously transforms diagnostic failures into new clinical capabilities through tool composition and task-specific model training. Inspired by clinical practice, MedRSI introduces two mechanisms for clinically aligned self-evolution. Clinical-cost-aware failure prioritization directs improvement toward errors according to their potential clinical consequences rather than frequency alone. Fast discovery with slow registration separates rapid capability invention from conservative adoption, allowing new tools to enter the persistent agent only after demonstrating sustained benefit across subsequent patient cohorts. Across public glaucoma and heart disease benchmarks and two private clinical tasks, MedRSI progressively develops segmentation, measurement, prediction, multimodal reasoning, and generative capabilities, surpasses manually engineered medical agents, and autonomously discovers solutions to clinical problems not anticipated by its original designers. Our results show that medical agents need not remain constrained by capabilities specified before deployment: with clinically grounded mechanisms governing what to improve and what to retain, they can continuously construct, validate, and accumulate new capabilities from diagnostic experience. Code is available at https://github.com/ImprintLab/MedRSI.

title: Ongeneeslijk zieke mama’s Ellen en Chloë maakten samen een kinderboek: “Het allerschoonste dat ik mijn zoontje kan nalaten”
content: Ellen Casteleyn (41) en Chloë Van Den Broecke (36) vonden elkaar toen ze allebei kanker kregen. Dezelfde ziekte, dezelfde behandeling, kinderen van bijna dezelfde leeftijd en uiteindelijk hetzelfde ongeneeslijke verdict. Het kinderboek dat ze samen maakten, heeft Chloë niet meer kunnen zien. “Haar dood heeft mij wakker geschud dat het voor mij ook snel kan gaan.”

title: Gavbangi: Iran’s Long-Running Conservation Effort Relies on Volunteers — and Turns Them Into Habitat Protectors
content:
Iran has experienced multiple crises over the past few years, including economic challenges and war. So far, however, these have not appeared to affect one of the most practical initiatives developed by local conservation leaders in northern Iran: Gavbangi.
In Farsi Gavbangi refers to the call of the maral (also known as Caspian red deer, Cervus elaphus maral), who live in the green mountains in northern Iran from early September to early October. Maral habitat in Iran spans forests from the Azerbaijan-Iran borderland in the northwest to Golestan National Park in the east.
In autumn the forests in the north display beautiful, colorful leaves, and local people commonly hear a sound like a cow that they call Gav (cow) bangi (call). It is both inspiring and reassuring to hear the charismatic calls of deer echoing through the forests, a reminder of a functioning ecosystem. As a former conservation volunteer in Iran and a current Ph.D. student in natural resources at the University of Vermont, I experienced Gavbangi in northern Iran’s protected areas. During that time I witnessed firsthand the vital role of community collaboration in maral’s conservation.
I have also seen the importance of this collaboration: Poachers know this is the ideal time to find deer, specifically males.
Maral are a protected species in Iran, but according to the Iranian Department of Environment they face two main threats: habitat loss and poaching. During Gavbangi volunteer conservationists collaborate with rangers and protected area managers to address both threats in protected areas and potential habitats.
Volunteers stay in scheduled locations across the habitat, listening to deer calls and ensuring that poachers do not take advantage of this vulnerable period. Volunteers are divided into small groups assigned to remote areas that are difficult to monitor with a small number of rangers. Their visible presence alone acts as an obstacle, discouraging poachers from entering.
These days economic pressure may be driving an increase in poaching, although there is no reliable data. Human development like expanding road networks also makes these efforts more critical than ever.
Social media and wildlife photography have played a significant role in promoting awareness of species and habitat protection in Iran. Many young volunteers became interested in conservation activities by seeing the beauty of nature and its residents.
The most interesting social aspect of Gavbangi is how volunteers gather. In my experience social media, activists, and the role of wildlife photographers are crucial, as they showcase the beauty of nature and its diverse forms. These individuals typically work closely with rangers to manage volunteers and identify the best locations. This is an excellent example of collaboration between the public sector and volunteer conservationists, which began around 15 years ago.
Many experts say it’s necessary to see interested individuals as an opportunity to preserve biodiversity. The main advantage of these activities is that they involve more people in conservation, which could lead to more effective conservation of the red deer.
There is an ongoing debate among conservationists about whether participation in Gavbangi should remain purely voluntary or be integrated into ecotourism programs, where participants pay to join. Although hosting a tour can bring money to the area and invest it in conservation, it can attract irresponsible individuals and increase the human population, which can negatively affect the project’s goal and compromise the area’s safety.
To me another aspect of Gavbangi is that it provides amateur volunteers with the opportunity to explore the ecosystem in the wild, which could be an excellent driver for enhancing conservation.
As a former volunteer turned professional conservationist, I feel it essential that volunteer initiatives like Gavbangi be closely monitored as they grow to ensure they stay on the right path, especially in engaging younger generations in protecting the Maral during its most vulnerable period. To achieve this, it would be beneficial if local conservation groups collaborate with conservation experts to train the volunteers. And Gavbangi leaders can benefit greatly from engaging local residents on conservation efforts.
Based on my conversations with several experts involved in Gavbangi, Iran’s ongoing challenges have not had a direct impact on the event so far. However, conservationists in the country are under considerable pressure, and we may see the effects of these crises in the next Gavbangi event.
It is our collective responsibility to ensure that future generations can still hear the haunting call of the deer echoing through the northern forests of Iran.

A Historic Milestone
Japan now has more than 100,000 people aged 100 or over. According to resident registration data from the Ministry of Health, Labor, and Welfare, the number of centenarians increased by 7,914 from the previous year to 107,677, as of September 1, 2026. This is the highest total since statistics were first collected in 1963, and the figure has risen for 56 consecutive years. Women account for an overwhelming majority at 94,298, or 87.6%, compared to 13,379 men.
Japan’s oldest woman is 114-year-old Kishimoto Fuyo, who lives in Kyoto. She is the last living Japanese born in the Meiji period (1868–1912). The oldest man in Japan is Katō Hikaru, aged 112 and living in Kumamoto.
In 1963, when the government enacted the Act on Social Welfare for the Elderly, there were 153 centenarians counted nationwide. That figure passed 1,000 in 1981 and 10,000 in 1998, and has continued to climb steadily since.
The prefecture with the highest ratio of centenarians per 100,000 people is Shimane at 186.7, which is more than three times as many as Saitama, the lowest at 51.3. Western Japan tends to have higher ratios than the east of the country, and figures are particularly low in the Kantō region, centered on the Tokyo metropolitan area.

title: Freedom: A Difficult Path That Comes at Women’s Cost
content:
I grew up in a house with mud walls and a low ceiling. From the small window of my room, I would always look at the sky over Kabul, a sky that seemed to me like a vast canvas. In a city that sometimes smelled of fear and insecurity, I had learned to seek refuge in the world of books. To me, every book was a window opening into another world, a world where no wall could stop the human mind from taking flight.
This is the story of a girl who had ambitious dreams but was buried and forgotten. In one of the remote provinces, where harmful traditions sometimes overshadow basic human principles, Zahra was a girl whose dreams were confined by the mud walls of her home. In that society, both hidden and open violence had taken root not only in the streets and markets but also in major family decisions.
Zahra’s father, under pressure from harmful social customs and in an attempt to resolve a long-standing dispute, decided to marry her off to a man many years older than her. Zahra, who dreamed of continuing her education and gaining knowledge, resisted the forced decision. But in a society where structural violence had deprived girls of the right to choose, her voice was lost amid the demands of the men making the decisions. Her father viewed marriage through misguided interpretations of tradition, not as a union based on consent and human dignity, but as a means of protecting his own “honor.”
On the day of the marriage ceremony, Zahra, her eyes red from hidden tears, witnessed a transaction in which her human dignity was disregarded. What she experienced was nothing less than the loss of her sense of self and freedom.
The marriage not only distanced Zahra from her dreams but also pushed her into a cycle of loneliness and despair. In a society where family relationships are shaped by violence and coercion, Zahra, living silently in her new home and enduring violence from her husband, was no longer the cheerful and ambitious girl she once was.
Then, one morning, the devastating news came: “Zahra had taken her own life.” Hearing those words, I trembled all over. What injustice had she suffered? Why had that intelligent girl reached such a desperate point? Why had she been forced into such a fate?
During those days, my only source of comfort was the small library I had in a corner of our home. With her limited education, my mother taught me that knowledge was not simply about reading words, but about gaining a deeper understanding of life. She always told me that instead of becoming consumed by the bitter side of life, I should search for its deeper meaning.
Kabul was a city of contradictions for me. Alongside poverty and hardship, there were still people who, despite living in poverty, had generous hearts and helped others. From them, I learned that humanity is not measured by wealth, but by the greatness of one’s spirit. This was one of life’s greatest lessons, one I learned from ordinary people in the city’s streets and alleys.
When the schools were closed, I did not lose hope. I told myself, “If the school is closed, my mind is still open.” I began writing. For me, writing was not a hobby, but a “silent uprising.” I wrote so I would not forget who I was or what I dreamed of. I wrote so that I could be the voice of all the girls who, in silence, were searching for a path toward the light.
During those difficult days, I thought about why human rights are sometimes disregarded in the country. I found the answer in “illiteracy” and “lack of awareness.” When a society moves away from knowledge, superstition and harmful traditions can take the place of truth. I decided to become part of that change. I did not want to be just a passive observer. I wanted to be someone who could use her pen to break down the walls of ignorance.
I thought about the value of informed marriage based on love and respect. A marriage in which two people come together as companions to build a dignified life, rather than as owner and owned. In Islam and its teachings centered on human dignity, mutual consent and respect for the dignity of both women and men are fundamental principles. I knew that if a society wanted to progress, it needed to return to these human principles.
Every morning when I woke up, I asked myself, “What will I learn today?” I began learning new skills. I wanted to become a woman who, when she entered society, would not only have something to say but would also know how to help address the problems facing her community.
Sometimes I was afraid of the insecurity in the city. But now, when I think about those days, I realize that freedom is not a gift; it is an achievement. Freedom is born in the moment when you decide that instead of giving in to sorrow, you will learn to give hope to others. I am no longer that frightened girl. I have become like the wind, finding its way through the rocks. I know that after every sunset, another sunrise will come.
Perhaps Kabul is a city of fear today, but I still believe in the dawn of liberation. Amid all this destruction, I stand and build. I have learned that even if the whole world stands against me, as long as I believe in myself, no wall can silence my voice. I am still moving forward, with fear and limitations, but with a heart that beats for freedom and awareness.

title: El rugido del mar: bioacústica comunitaria para entender cómo el cambio climático afecta al pez mero del Caribe en México
content:
- En Punta Allen, Quintana Roo, miembros del Centro Comunitario de Investigación y Monitoreo Submarino (CECIMS) monitorean al mero del Caribe (Epinephelus striatus) con hidrófonos que escuchan su actividad durante la época de reproducción.
- Desde que la comunidad creó dos Zonas de Refugio Pesquero en 2016, las agregaciones reproductivas del mero han repuntado en un sitio casi extinto, registrando hasta 100 individuos por buceo y más de 1800 en el sitio de mayor presencia.
- La especie está en peligro crítico de extinción: desova cada año en los mismos sitios y bajo la misma luna, una constancia que facilita su sobrepesca: de los 28 sitios de agregación que recuerdan los pescadores, hoy solo seis están validados científicamente.
- Los sensores oceanográficos del CECIMS han documentado un aumento de al menos un grado en la temperatura del agua en una década, y durante el blanqueamiento masivo de corales de 2023-2024, el peor registrado a nivel mundial, captaron los picos de calentamiento en tiempo real.
Treinta metros bajo la superficie del mar, un sonido reverbera por el arrecife. Cientos de meros del Caribe (Epinephelus striatus) se congregan en un frenesí de cortejo que sucede una sola vez al año. Vocalizan. Cambian de color. Danzan en espiral unos alrededor de otros. El propósito: asegurar su reproducción. Su rugido particular se mezcla con otro sonido que resalta entre el bullicio. Con el regulador todavía puesto, Magdiel ‘Mako’ Naal, buzo y monitor comunitario, grita: «¡Ya se está recuperando San Juan!».
Este frenesí reproductivo y sonoro sucede en uno de los reservorios de biodiversidad más importantes de México: la Reserva de la Biosfera de Sian Ka’an, cuyo nombre significa ‘el origen del cielo’ en lengua maya. La reserva abarca más de 650 000 hectáreas de selva tropical, manglares y humedales que colindan con el Sistema Arrecifal Mesoamericano (SAM), la segunda barrera de coral más grande del mundo. El sitio es Patrimonio de la Humanidad declarado por la UNESCO desde 1987 y alberga una comunidad que existe mucho antes de su nombramiento. Punta Allen y sus 400 habitantes sostienen la historia de la cooperativa pesquera Vigía Chico.
En 2015, pescadoras y pescadores de la cooperativa se organizaron para crear el Centro Comunitario de Investigación y Monitoreo Submarino (CECIMS), el primero de su tipo en la región. Desde entonces, generan información científica que sustenta la renovación de dos Zonas de Refugio Pesquero en la Reserva, ubicada en el estado de Quintana Roo. Estos refugios son áreas protegidas federales que la propia comunidad propone, estudia y defiende. Para ello utilizan el monitoreo acústico pasivo: hidrófonos colocados en el fondo del arrecife que escuchan al mero durante su época de reproducción.
Entre 2017 y 2025 acumularon más de 8000 minutos de grabaciones submarinas y lograron registrar los diferentes sonidos de los peces, al punto de identificar con precisión las fechas de desove. Desde la implementación de los refugios, la cantidad de meros que llegan hasta la zona para reproducirse ha crecido, registrando hasta 3000 individuos por temporada en el sitio de mayor abundancia.
El mero del Caribe —también conocido como mero de Nassau o mero estriado— se encuentra en lo alto de la cadena alimenticia, justo por debajo de los tiburones. Es una especie importante para estos arrecifes, pero también una de las más vulnerables. Clasificado en Peligro Crítico de extinción por la Unión Internacional para la Conservación de la Naturaleza (UICN), es solitario la mayor parte de su vida, pero entre enero y marzo abandona el aislamiento para congregarse de a miles en sitios específicos del arrecife y desovar bajo la luna llena. Siempre el mismo sitio y la misma luna. A estos eventos se les llama “agregaciones reproductivas”. Sin embargo, esa constancia que hace posible su reproducción también ha facilitado su sobrepesca y algunos de estos sitios ya han sido exterminados.
Científicos han identificado seis sitios de agregación en Quintana Roo, pero no fueron los primeros en hacerlo. Los pescadores más antiguos hablan de 28 sitios donde sucede —o sucedía— el espectáculo reproductivo. Uno de ellos es San Juan, que hoy es una de las dos Zonas de Refugio Pesquero que protege la cooperativa. Antes de que se prohibiera la extracción de especies durante los meses de las agregaciones reproductivas, cuentan en Punta Allen, los furtivos pescaban con dinamita y extrajeron toneladas de mero hasta acabar con ellos. En 2016, cuando la comunidad logró la creación del refugio, el sitio estaba dado por perdido. Una década de vigilancia y monitoreo más tarde, este año se volvieron a registrar más de cien meros del Caribe en la zona: una señal de que San Juan revive.
Pero lo que es una gran historia de éxito para los meros y los pobladores de Punta Allen está en peligro por una nueva amenaza: la crisis climática.
Los “meros-meros” del Caribe
«Es como un ronquido, como un rugido bastante grave. Rápidamente lo identificas porque no eres tú ni el compañero. Volteas y ahí está. Te está viendo y te está avisando que estás entrando en su zona». Así describe Magdiel Naal el encuentro con un mero del Caribe durante los buceos.
Naal es de los pocos nacidos en Punta Allen y actualmente sostiene la presidencia del CECIMS. El mar no es nada nuevo para él. «De pequeño me escapaba de la escuela y me escondía en la lancha de mi papá. Cuando se daban cuenta ya estábamos en altamar», recuerda. Su padre, Daniel, fue uno de los primeros buzos monitores de Punta Allen, de los que salieron a buscar las agregaciones de mero cuando nadie sabía bien qué eran ni para qué servían; mientras que su hijo, Jorge, comenzó a monitorear con solo 10 años y hoy, a los 22, es buzo de rescate y forma parte de la cuarta generación de monitores. «El mar te llama; quieres sentir la emoción de estar allá afuera», afirma Magdiel Naal.
A diferencia de las áreas marinas protegidas, que se establecen por decreto presidencial, las Zonas de Refugio Pesquero son una solución de las comunidades para las comunidades. Consideradas en la Ley General de Pesca y Acuacultura Sustentables, son propuestas por los propios pescadores y miembros de la comunidad, quienes definen qué especie proteger, en qué sitio y con qué objetivo. Pero no son un acuerdo opcional: sus reglas se publican en el Diario Oficial de la Federación y obligan a todos a seguirlas. Una vez aprobadas, tienen una duración de cinco años y deben renovarse con una justificación científica, explica Omar Rivera, mentor de cambio en Comunidad y Biodiversidad (COBI), una asociación civil que ha apoyado a cerca del 80 % de los refugios pesqueros mexicanos.
En Punta Allen hay dos zonas de refugio pesquero: Niche Habin y San Juan, que miden entre 15 y 17 km2 y van desde los 20 a los 100 metros de profundidad. Ambas se han renovado dos veces y buscan la protección de las agregaciones reproductivas del mero del Caribe. Para lograrlo, queda prohibido pescar mero durante la temporada de reproducción dentro de los polígonos marcados, y son los comités de vigilancia de la propia cooperativa quienes hacen cumplir la norma.
Pero el refugio pesquero es más que una figura legal. «Sirve como un faro», dice Rivera. «Ese faro trae una luz que ilumina muchas otras actividades». Desde su implementación, las zonas de refugio han fortalecido las capacidades técnicas y científicas de la comunidad, generado espacios de participación igualitaria dentro de la cooperativa, y transferido liderazgo a nuevas generaciones, sostiene el biólogo. En la práctica, cinco de los once miembros del CECIMS son mujeres y ya van cuatro generaciones de líderes comunitarios que se forman en buceo, monitoreo y conservación.
Distinguir el rugido del mero entre el ruido del arrecife en los miles de minutos de grabaciones exige una ayuda tecnológica que la comunidad por sí sola no puede construir. Por eso, el CECIMS y COBI se aliaron con el investigador Laurent M. Cherubin, de la Florida Atlantic University, para implementar un programa capaz de reconocer y aislar el sonido de las distintas especies de mero. Los hidrófonos se quedan uno o dos meses en el fondo del mar; después, las grabaciones son procesadas en Estados Unidos, el algoritmo separa las vocalizaciones del mero del resto del bullicio y los datos vuelven a Punta Allen convertidos en fechas y horas de actividad reproductiva clasificadas por especie. Es precisamente este resultado el que le permite a la cooperativa “espiar” a los meros durante las agregaciones reproductivas sin el costo ni el riesgo de bucear una y otra vez a 30 metros de profundidad.
Cuando las primeras grabaciones fueron analizadas por los investigadores en Florida, su programa identificó miles de meros tigre (Mycteroperca tigris) o alguna otra especie del género Mycteroperca. «Les dijimos: no es cierto, tu programa te está diciendo una mentira, no hemos visto más que dos o tres meros tigre en comparación con los miles de meros del Caribe que vemos durante las agregaciones», cuenta Rivera. En ese momento descubrieron que los meros del Caribe mexicano vocalizan diferente a los meros del Caribe estadounidense. Misma especie, distinto acento. Tan distinto que Rivera no descarta que futuros análisis genéticos revelen subespecies.
Esto llevó a que los investigadores recalibraran el algoritmo. Desde entonces, los datos regresan a Punta Allen procesados y precisos.
Esa precisión permite algo que antes era imposible: saber, sin bajar al agua, si la agregación reproductiva ya comenzó. «Ahí vemos la gráfica: en qué día, a qué hora, en qué fase de la luna», dice Magdiel Naal. Los hidrófonos también confirmaron algo que los pescadores más viejos ya intuían: al caer el sol, la actividad reproductiva se intensifica. «Se ponen más románticos en la tarde-noche», comenta Rivera.
Los informes se presentan cada año en asamblea ante toda la cooperativa y también se comparten con las autoridades gubernamentales que gestionan la reserva de Sian Ka’an. «Al principio no nos tomaban en cuenta», dice Naal sobre los directivos de la cooperativa. «Ya empezamos a mostrarles qué hacemos. Ahora ellos mismos preguntan: ‘¿cuántos viste?’ Nosotros se los presentamos: ‘esto es lo que vemos, esto es lo que escuchamos y esto es lo que pasa’. Con esa información [los directivos de la cooperativa] dicen: ‘okey, [están funcionando las zonas de refugio pesquero] vamos a renovar'».
¿Mal clima para los meros?
«Tu mente no entiende lo que tu vista ve», dice Lucía Cosgaya. Lleva dos temporadas buceando en las zonas de refugio pesquero de Punta Allen y recuerda así la primera vez que descendió a una agregación reproductiva de mero en Niche Habin. Contó 150 individuos en un cuadro mental y se rindió —eran miles—. Cosgaya no es bióloga ni pescadora, pero conoce los altibajos del mar mejor que muchos. Ella es cocinera tradicional, madre, vecina de la comunidad y esposa de un socio de la cooperativa que también es monitor del CECIMS.
Durante años vio salir a los buzos desde la orilla sin ser una de ellos, pues sus múltiples responsabilidades se entrelazaban con el prejuicio hacia la mujer en los entornos marinos. “De pequeña ni me dejaban esnorquelear”, cuenta. Hoy es monitora comunitaria del CECIMS y bucea a 30 metros de profundidad en condiciones que no son nada sencillas. “El miedo no se ha ido del todo. Cuando dicen ‘agregación’ empieza a retumbar mi corazón. Pero si logro entrar, todo cambia», dice Cosgaya. “Rompes tus barreras, rompes tus miedos. Te vuelves poderosa”.
Las agregaciones no ocurren en cualquier condición. «Solo están ahí cuando hay mal clima», sostiene Cosgaya. Y eso, «tiene una lógica aplastante» para la buceadora. El oleaje y las corrientes no son un obstáculo sino una necesidad biológica. Las larvas del mero logran dispersarse gracias a las fuertes corrientes que acompañan un “mal clima”. Estas condiciones les permiten alejarse de los depredadores y sobrevivir. Mientras que para los meros, el mal clima les permite subsistir, para los monitores, la travesía al sitio puede tomar más de una hora en esas condiciones difíciles. «La última vez que fuimos, un capitán quería regresar y el otro no», cuenta.
Sin embargo, lo que el cambio climático amenaza no es solo la temperatura del arrecife sino esta lógica de supervivencia: Si los patrones de corrientes se alteran, la dispersión de larvas se ve comprometida y con ella la variabilidad genética del mero del Caribe.
Un estudio de 2018 ya mostraba la fuerte relación entre calentamiento del océano, cambios en las corrientes marinas y en las agregaciones reproductivas del mero del Caribe. Ese calentamiento puede transformar las condiciones físicas que sostienen la reproducción del pez en el Gran Caribe y sus conexiones con el golfo de México. Al elevar la temperatura superficial del mar, el agua se vuelve menos densa y puede modificar la dinámica de las corrientes. Estos cambios son relevantes porque las agregaciones de desove de la especie se asocian con un intervalo térmico relativamente estrecho —entre 24 y 27.5 °C— y con determinadas condiciones de circulación. El estudio señala que el hábitat adecuado para las agregaciones reproductivas podría disminuir y desplazarse hacia el norte: una señal de alerta para una especie cuya reproducción depende de encuentros masivos, breves y sincronizados en sitios específicos.
Por eso, los sensores oceanográficos del CECIMS llevan una década registrando la temperatura del agua en los sitios de agregación y han documentado un cambio de al menos un grado en ese período. En los episodios más cálidos han llegado a marcar 31.5 grados centígrados a 30 metros de profundidad. Durante el blanqueamiento masivo de corales en 2023-2024 —el más grave hasta la fecha, pues afectó a más del 84 % de los arrecifes del mundo, incluido el SAM, según la NOAA— los sensores de Punta Allen captaron los picos de calentamiento en tiempo real. «Hemos visto cambios en los corales, como blanqueamiento y nuevas enfermedades», dice Lucía Cosgaya. Para ella, la consecuencia es obvia: “Dependemos de los corales. Si no hay corales vivos, no hay peces».

En las asambleas comunitarias, los datos dejan de ser sólo gráficas que reúnen temperatura, fecha, hora y actividad vocal del mero: se convierten en historias que tocan lo que sucede fuera del agua. «Para la gente no solo el agua estaba caliente», explica Rivera. El aire y el cuerpo también: «hubo menos pesca, más enfermedades y no sirvió la planta de luz en ciertos días». Los efectos del cambio climático y la sobrepesca no se los vienen a contar: los escuchan, los ven y los viven en su comunidad. Por lo mismo, «el conocimiento que a veces tanto nos gusta presumir, ellos lo tienen de una manera tan natural que no lo necesitan alardear», dice el biólogo. Este conocimiento anclado al territorio, sumado al dato preciso que la ciencia les ofrece, ha probado ser un gran aliado para la protección de su hogar.
Lo que a Rivera más le impacta es que, «a pesar de que son personas que llevan toda la vida viviendo allá, está esa capacidad de asombro, esa capacidad de orgullo de lo que representan esos sitios [de reproducción del mero del Caribe] para ellos». A Punta Allen la sostienen cuatro generaciones de pescadores que aprendieron a escuchar al mar incluso antes de que se interpretaran los datos. Ahora esos datos les devuelven lo que sus mayores intuían mirando la luna y las estrellas: el momento exacto en que el mero se reúne a cantar, danzar y desovar. «El mar representa todo para nosotros», dice Lucía Cosgaya. «El mar es vida», dice Magdiel Naal. «Un lugar estable, si lo cuidas», dice Jorge Naal. Daniel Naal no agrega nada más, solo escucha las olas.
Un Estado que no colabora
Durante todo el año el mero suele mostrar una coloración café-rojiza con barras claras. Pero en las agregaciones reproductivas su cuerpo cambia: aparecen fases adicionales —bicolor, oscura, de vientre claro—. En la zona, estudios recientes han documentado que esas fases son un lenguaje corporal con el que los peces coordinan el cortejo, la territorialidad, la disponibilidad reproductiva y, posiblemente, los roles dentro del desove. «Es como cuando ves a un ave hacer danzas aquí en la tierra, ahí abajo ves a los meros cortejando y danzando», describe Rivera. Al caer la tarde, el cortejo culmina: un grupo asciende de golpe y, al frente, una hembra libera los huevos mientras detrás los machos los fertilizan.
La norma mexicana que regula el aprovechamiento del mero abarca las costas del Golfo de México y el Caribe, pero fue diseñada en torno al mero rojo (Epinephelus morio), una especie que destaca en las pesquerías del Golfo pero que escasea en las del Caribe. De ahí vienen dos desajustes para el mero del Caribe. El primero, de talla: la norma fija una talla mínima de captura de 36.3 centímetros —por debajo de los 38 a 50 en que el mero del Caribe alcanza la madurez—, de modo que permite pescarlo antes de que llegue a reproducirse. El segundo, de calendario: la veda vigente para el Caribe mexicano va del 1° de febrero al 31 de marzo; y con el cambio climático, las fechas de desove cambian, señalan los investigadores. «La época de veda está desfasada», advierte Rivera. «Hemos visto que todavía hay meros en etapa de reproducción en meses en que la veda ya no está activa».
Para corregir los datos, COBI, junto con la Asociación Interamericana para la Defensa del Ambiente (AIDA) y el Fondo para el Sistema Arrecifal Mesoamericano (MAR Fund), recomiendan aumentar la talla mínima para incluir la talla de madurez del mero del Caribe, separar la veda del Golfo de la del Caribe y extender la de esta última región de dos a cuatro meses. También proponen reconocer oficialmente las agregaciones reproductivas como sitios de importancia crítica en la legislación pesquera mexicana, otro vacío que persiste. Un investigador de la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) trabaja actualmente en una propuesta para ajustar esa época de veda con base en los datos acústicos del CECIMS.
Los datos que recogen los pescadores mantienen de pie un refugio que le da a los meros la seguridad para multiplicarse. Con esa información, el CECIMS le comprueba a la cooperativa que los refugios funcionan y ésta destina más recursos para su renovación y vigilancia. Rivera explica que, según un informe reciente, se han logrado identificar y detener a más de cincuenta personas por pesca ilegal en la zona.
Y los meros notan la creciente protección: En Niche Habin las temporadas vuelven a reunir miles de meros; en San Juan, que pasó varios años sin ver un solo pez, ya empieza a repoblarse. «Todos estos factores sociales de gobernanza por parte de la comunidad, combinados con que existe un polígono de protección oficial, están haciendo su chamba [su trabajo]», dice Rivera.
Pero la Reserva de la Biosfera de Sian Ka’an y la comunidad costera de Punta Allen no están exentas de otras amenazas. Desde Tulum, uno de los polos de desarrollo más cercanos a la reserva, llegan la contaminación y los pescadores furtivos que activamente buscan los sitios con mayor biodiversidad. «Si se enteran de que hay un lugar bonito, ahí ya valió [ya no tiene futuro]», dice Jorge Naal, hijo de Magdiel y miembro de la cuarta generación de buzos monitores del CECIMS y quien ya cría a la quinta.
El proyecto Puerta al Mar —una carretera de 54 kilómetros que el Ejército mexicano construye a través de los humedales de Sian Ka’an hacia el Mar Caribe, y que incluye restaurantes, muelle y una playa artificial sobre manglares— preocupa a la comunidad por el modelo de desarrollo que podría atraer hacia las zonas de refugio. «Tiene implicaciones directas», advierte Rivera. «La intención de traer un modelo de desarrollo no compatible con lo que quieren las comunidades es una amenaza, sin duda». La cooperativa se ha opuesto formalmente al proyecto, asegura Magdiel Naal.
Daniel Naal tiene más de 40 años en Punta Allen. Ya no bucea, su columna se lo impide. Se le atribuye haber inventado la sombra para langostas, ese método ahora reconocido por su eficacia y utilizado en todo el Caribe para la pesca sostenible de estos crustáceos. Él fue uno de los primeros del pueblo en capacitarse como buzo y monitor comunitario, cuando nadie sabía a ciencia cierta qué era una agregación reproductiva ni para qué servía monitorearla. Hoy, su hijo Magdiel preside el CECIMS, su nieto Jorge ya participa en los monitoreos y acaba de convertirse en padre. «Ojalá crezca y conozca la especie», dice Daniel sobre su bisnieto. «Esto que hacemos es para las futuras generaciones, no para nosotros que ya vamos de salida».
*Imagen principal: Epinephelus striatus en su coloración café-rojiza. El mero del Caribe nace con gónadas sin una sexualidad definida. Hacia los cuatro o cinco años alcanza la madurez sexual y se establece como hembra o macho, un mecanismo poco estudiado. Foto: cortesía MarAlliance

title: Keiko Fujimori anuncia relanzamiento de programa Sierra Verde con inversión de US$30 millones para reforzar 50 mil hectáreas en los Andes
content:
Keiko Fujimori, presidenta del Perú, anunció en Nueva York el relanzamiento del programa Sierra Verde, que contempla una inversión de US$300 millones durante los próximos cinco años y tiene como meta reforestar 50 mil hectáreas en los Andes del Perú.
Keiko Fujimori, presidenta del Perú, anunció en Nueva York el relanzamiento del programa Sierra Verde, que contempla una inversión de US$300 millones durante los próximos cinco años y tiene como meta reforestar 50 mil hectáreas en los Andes del Perú.
El anuncio fue realizado durante el encuentro organizado por Rainforest Alliance denominado “Invirtiendo en el Perú del Futuro: Sostenibilidad, Competitividad y Liderazgo Climático Global a través de sus Comunidades Campesinas e Indígenas”, desarrollado en el marco de la Semana de Alto Nivel del 81.º período de sesiones de la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas.
Durante su intervención, la mandataria explicó que el proyecto permitirá generar más de 350 mil puestos de trabajo, preservar 100 millones de metros cúbicos de agua subterránea y beneficiar a 100 comunidades. Asimismo, indicó que la propuesta busca aprovechar la riqueza natural del país para impulsar el desarrollo productivo de los Andes.
“Perú es un país con una inmensa riqueza nacional y diversidad, uno de los mejores en el planeta, desde la costa, andes y la Amazonía, que alberga una extraordinaria combinación de recursos marinos, amazonia, suelo y biodiversidad. Queremos que esta extraordinaria riqueza natural esté presente en un lugar diferente en nuestra estrategia de desarrollo”, expresó.
Fujimori resaltó que el país cuenta con una base sobre la cual impulsar esta estrategia, que comprende políticas públicas, inversión, compromisos ambientales, conocimiento científico y la participación de las poblaciones asentadas en estos territorios.
“No estamos empezando desde cero. Perú ya tiene políticas, programas, inversión pública, mecanismos de ecosistema de servicios, compromisos climáticos, conocimiento científico y una extraordinaria experiencia y liderazgo de nuestras comunidades indígenas y comunidades rurales”, remarcó.
En esa línea, explicó que Sierra Verde está orientado a recuperar el agua, mejorar las tierras y fortalecer los sistemas productivos de las comunidades mediante acciones de reforestación y manejo de los ecosistemas.

title: Afghan Minaret Restoration Marks 'Pragmatic' Taliban Approach To Cultural Heritage, Experts Say
content:
Restoration work under way on Afghanistan's most famous minaret is the latest indication that the country's Taliban rulers are taking a calculated approach to cultural heritage, in contrast to their statue-smashing predecessors of the 1990s, experts say.
Images of work to safeguard the UNESCO-listed Minaret of Jam emerged in mid September when a Taliban official visited the 12th-century monument, located in an isolated valley of Afghanistan’s Ghor Province, to check on rehabilitation efforts that reportedly began in July.
A spokesperson linked to the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, which is working on the landmark in cooperation with several other organizations, told RFE/RL that the project includes “emergency intervention to consolidate a critical section of the inner masonry column at the base of the minaret.” The isolated brick structure was repeatedly damaged by flooding and had long been in danger of collapse.
Jolyon Leslie is a British conservation architect who has lived in Afghanistan since the early 1990s and dealt with the first Taliban that ruled over Afghanistan from 1996-2001.
Leslie told RFE/RL that the country's current rulers appear to be “more worldly about cultural issues, and conscious of their image in being seen to protect their heritage” when compared to the previous Taliban rulers.
The heritage protection expert with the Afghan Cultural Heritage Consulting Organization added that in his organization's experience "since 2021 [the Taliban authorities have] been largely supportive of conservation work and have not interfered in our work, which has included Buddhist and Jewish heritage.”
In February 2001, Afghanistan's first Taliban leaders ordered the destruction of statues and non-Islamic shrines in the country. The edict was followed most infamously by the destruction of the Bamiyan buddhas, and the smashing of thousands of ancient statues in Kabul's National Museum of Afghanistan, months before the Taliban were ousted from power.
Soon after the Taliban retook control of Afghanistan in 2021, Leslie was the only Westerner in attendance at a meeting in the Kabul museum, during which he later recalled a Taliban official hinted at regret over the 2001 destruction, due to the global outrage it caused.
Gil Stein, a professor of archaeology at the University of Chicago who led efforts to restore the smashed museum statues, notes that the current Taliban’s approach to cultural heritage stands in marked contrast to other facets of the hardline group’s rule.
“Like everything about Afghanistan, the situation is complex and contradictory. The most basic principle is that we cannot consider the Taliban government as unitary and monolithic,” Stein told RFE/RL. “That’s a big part of why there are major differences between Taliban policies on women (which are draconian) versus their policies on cultural heritage (which are more nuanced and differing by region and by distance from Kabul).”
The Taliban has severely restricted rights for women and girls, including limiting their ability to work and study, and mandating they be covered from head to toe in public.
The change in rhetoric over cultural heritage preceded the current Taliban's return to power. In February 2021, months before their capture of Kabul, the resurgent militant group issued an edict calling for “all mujahedeen” to “preserve all historic sites like old fortresses, minarets, towers and other similar sites to safeguard them from damage, destruction and decay.”
Many viewed the edict with suspicion and, as the Taliban advanced toward Kabul in 2021, some museum curators urgently relocated cultural treasures to secret storage locations.
But soon after the fall of Kabul in 2021 the National Museum was reopened -- under armed Taliban guard -- and multiple restoration projects have since been greenlit, including a synagogue in Herat Province in western Afghanistan.
"Overall, it looks to me that the Taliban's overall ideology has not changed, but they have become more pragmatic and careful in how they implement their cultural heritage policies in the places where it is most visible to foreigners," Stein said, in answer to questions about the restoration of the Minaret of Jam.
According to the Aga Khan Development Network, research on the minaret is being carried out in partnership with Afghanistan’s Taliban-run Culture Ministry and the ALIPH Foundation, a Geneva-based cultural heritage organization. The research is due to conclude in 2027 and “will result in recommendations to the Afghan authorities on further scientific measures required to secure the site.”

title: تفاؤل حكومي في مصر بنجاح خطة «تقليل الإنجاب»
content:
جاء إعلان الجهاز المركزي للتعبئة العامة والإحصاء في مصر عن انخفاض معدلات المواليد بنسبة 18.2 في المائة، مصحوباً بحالة من التفاؤل لدى المؤسسات الحكومية المعنية بقضية الزيادة السكانية، بما يُعطي انطباعاً بنجاح خطة «تقليل الإنجاب» وبرامج «تنظيم الأسرة» التي تبنتها مصر، وواصلت تنفيذها على مدى نحو 40 عاماً.
وأعلن رئيس الجهاز المركزي للتعبئة العامة والإحصاء، أكرم الجوهري، عن انخفاض مستويات الإنجاب في مصر بنسبة 18.2 في المائة، إذ بلغ متوسط عدد الأطفال لكل سيدة 2.33 طفل، وفقاً للنتائج الأولية للمسح الصحي للأسرة المصرية لعام 2025، مقارنةً بـ2.85 طفل في عام 2021.
وقال، خلال مؤتمر «إعلان نتائج المسح الصحي للأسرة المصرية 2025»، إن المسح نُفذ بالتعاون مع وزارتي الصحة والتخطيط، مشيراً إلى أنه يأتي امتداداً لسلسلة المسوح السكانية الصحية التي أُجريت في مصر خلال الفترة من 1988 إلى 2014.
وقال وزير التخطيط والتنمية الاقتصادية في مصر، أحمد رستم، إن المسح الصحي للأسرة المصرية يكتسب أهمية خاصة، لما يوفره من مؤشرات دقيقة حول الأوضاع الصحية والسكانية، وصحة الأم والطفل، والصحة الإنجابية، والتغذية، وغيرها من المؤشرات التي تمثل مرجعاً أساسياً في صياغة السياسات السكانية والصحية والاجتماعية.
وأكد الوزير في كلمته بالمؤتمر أن «نتائج هذا المسح تُمثل قاعدة معرفية تدعم تقييم فعالية البرامج الحكومية والسياسات الصحية والسكانية، وتُسهم في توجيه التدخلات التنموية إلى الفئات والمناطق الأكثر احتياجاً، فضلاً عن دعم تصميم السياسات المستقبلية القائمة على الأدلة، بما يتوافق مع أولويات الدولة المصرية ورؤية مصر 2030».
ويرى الدكتور صلاح سلام، نقيب الأطباء سابقاً بشمال سيناء، أن «هذه المعدلات لا أعتقد أنها تُشير إلى نجاح خطة تنظيم الأسرة بقدر كونها ترتبط بانخفاض معدلات الدخل».
وأضاف سلام لـ«الشرق الأوسط» أن «خفض معدلات الإنجاب بوصفه هدفاً للدولة ربما لا يرتبط ببرامج مدروسة لتنظيم الأسرة، كما حدث في عامي 1996 و2002، والتي أسهمت في خفض معدلات الإنجاب إلى نحو 2.8، فيما كان المستهدف 2.2. لكن ربما يكون السبب هو انخفاض مستويات الدخل، ما يدفع الأسر إلى التفكير كثيراً قبل الإنجاب، في ظل ارتفاع تكاليف العلاج والتعليم، وارتفاع تكلفة الحياة عموماً. وهذا، في رأيي، أحد الأسباب الرئيسية لانخفاض معدلات الإنجاب».
وكان وزير التخطيط والتنمية الاقتصادية قد شدد على أن نتائج المسح وما توفره من بيانات تأتي في إطار توجه الدولة المصرية إلى إيلاء قطاع الصحة أولوية قصوى؛ ولذلك تحرص الدولة على توجيه الاستثمارات العامة إلى هذا القطاع، إذ بلغ حجم الاستثمارات العامة المخصصة له في خطة 2026-2027 نحو 108 مليارات جنيه (الدولار يساوي نحو 52 جنيهاً مصرياً)، بزيادة تُقدّر بنحو 27 في المائة عن العام السابق.
وكانت مصر قد أطلقت عدداً من الحملات التوعوية لتنظيم الأسرة عبر تقليل الإنجاب، حفاظاً على المعدلات السكانية الملائمة للموارد، ومن بينها حملات دعائية أطلقت في الثمانينات والتسعينات من القرن الماضي، بعد طفرات في الزيادة السكانية التي شهدتها مصر من 26 مليون نسمة عام 1960 إلى 58 مليون نسمة عام 1990، في حين سجل عدد سكان مصر 109 ملايين نسمة في مايو (أيار) الماضي.

title: Grey Lynn and Ponsonby: From working class roots to Auckland's most sought after suburbs
content:
The evolution of Auckland’s inner suburbs
Auckland's villa-lined and leafy central suburbs are some of the city's most sought after and expensive, with the trendiest cafes and bars.
But Grey Lynn and Ponsonby were once working class areas, home to Pasifika communities and a social justice movement.
RNZ spoke to some of the people who have hung on through all of the changes.
One of them is Josephina Faiva - she has been living in her family home on Richmond Road for nearly 50 years - her family bought the house when they moved from Tonga when she was 17.
"A lot of a different Island people were in the area and now they all moved out and White man moved in. They've got the money and they move in."
As living nearer to the city became more desirable, house prices and rents shot up through the 1980s and 1990s and much of the Pasifika community was pushed to South Auckland.
But, Josephina's family stayed put, and she said despite having to travel to South Auckland to visit extended family, she still loved living in the area.
"We're sitting in the cafe, mostly with my White friends for coffee, and we get on very well."
Tigilau Ness was a member of the Polynesian Panthers, a social justice movement which was an important part of Ponsonby's history in the 1970s.
They were formed to fight against racism across society - including the infamous dawn raids, Ness said.
"It was a scary time for us. For Polynesians, and as Polynesian Panthers we stood up against it. We were dead set against any policy like that. It was state sanctioned terrorism to us."
Ness said there were illegal speakeasies run by gangs in Ponsonby at the time, which many young people frequented.
The Polynesian Panthers aimed to offer a more positive community, he said, offering homework centres and legal aid.
Ness had lived in the area for most of his life - but he found out this year his home on Ivanhoe Road would be forcibly bought out by the Transport Agency as part of the Northwestern busway project.
He was "hoping to" buy again in the area, but was unsure if he and his wife would be able to afford it.
"We've had a look around already. It's all in the $1 million + area, and we don't want to move in to apartments."
Local artist John Reynolds had lived in his house Richmond Road since the 1980s. He remembered a dairy owned by an "old communist" named George across the road.
"George was a wonderful character, and he'd go out the back if I mentioned communism, and bring out old Soviet magazines, like propaganda."
Reynolds said the building where George's dairy used to be was now a French wine bar.
He said that was great for people like him - but it was a good example of the sad, though inevitable change in the fabric of the neighbourhood over the years.

title: Beyond Centralized Policy Decision Points: Decentralized Sticky Policy Authorization through Evidence Quorums
content: Sticky policies remain attached to protected data so that access restrictions can persist across systems, yet request-time authorization often still depends on a centralized Trusted Authority or Policy Decision Point (PDP). This paper presents SPEAR-Q, a decentralized framework in which independent Policy Authority Nodes (PANs) evaluate the active sticky policy using local context, consent, and risk information and generate signed authorization evidence. A strict-majority Evidence quorum determines the global Permit or Deny decision, while a committed policy becomes active only after the required PAN majority applies it. SPEAR-Q was deployed across physically separated hosts in the Airbus Cyber Security Simulation Platform and evaluated using a healthcare workload derived from MIMIC-IV. Across 9,000 performance requests, all requests completed without execution failure or timeout. Latency increased and throughput saturated as cluster size and concurrency grew, with PAN evidence waiting and PAN-local processing dominating under load and credential validation forming the main PAN-side cost. Policy-activation experiments confirmed majority-based activation. Quorum experiments showed that correctly signed false-Permit evidence from fewer compromised PANs than the required quorum could not produce a global Permit or resource release, while authorization remained fail-closed when reachable PANs fell below the required quorum. Compared with prior approaches that decentralize policy management, credential authority, or threshold-based release separately, SPEAR-Q integrates persistent sticky policy enforcement, independent request-time evidence, majority-based policy activation, and explicit quorum-bounded authorization within one decentralized framework. Under the evaluated conditions, SPEAR-Q supports decentralized sticky-policy authorization without relying on a centralized decision authority.

title: Florida used robot rabbits to hunt Burmese pythons threatening the Everglades
content:
Florida used an unusual tool to control the growing population of invasive Burmese pythons in the Everglades: solar-powered robot rabbits. In 2025, the South Florida Water Management District and the University of Florida teamed up to deploy robotic rabbit decoys designed to mimic real prey and lure pythons out of hiding using artificial intelligence (AI), heat signatures and scent simulation.
The robots are part of Florida’s broader effort to remove Burmese pythons, which have disrupted native wildlife populations across the state. The devices use AI-powered cameras to detect approaching snakes and alert officials, who can then send trained python removal agents to capture and remove them. The technology is being used alongside the annual Florida Python Challenge and other removal programmes, not replacing them.
How Florida’s AI-powered robot rabbits work
The solar-powered robots are designed to imitate prey that Burmese pythons hunt. They produce a heat signature and emit a scent intended to attract the snakes, which use thermal sensing and smell while hunting. Each robot has an AI-powered camera that monitors the surrounding area. When it detects a python approaching, the system alerts South Florida Water Management District officials. A trained python removal agent can then be dispatched to the location.
The district and University of Florida are deploying the robots at sites across South Florida where pythons are known to hide. The approach is intended to help monitor areas that can be difficult to survey using conventional methods.
“These innovative robots produce a heat signature and emit a smell designed to attract pythons. The robots are equipped with cameras that monitor for pythons and notify District officials when a snake is detected. Once notified, the District can dispatch a python removal agent to the area,” the district noted.
Why Florida is targeting Burmese pythons
Burmese pythons were introduced into the Everglades during the 1970s and have since become an invasive predator in Florida. Researchers estimate that between 100,000 and 300,000 Burmese pythons are present across the state’s subtropical regions. The snakes can grow longer than 18 feet, and adult females can lay more than 70 eggs in a single clutch. Their presence has affected native mammals, birds and reptiles, reducing available prey for species including Florida panthers, bobcats and birds of prey.
A 2012 US Geological Survey study found that raccoon and opossum populations in parts of the Everglades had declined by nearly 99% following the spread of Burmese pythons.
Florida Python Challenge adds to python removal efforts
Florida has also relied on trained contractors and public participation to remove Burmese pythons. The annual Florida Python Challenge brings professional and amateur hunters together for a 10-day competition, and participants must complete a safety course before taking part. In the 2026 challenge, 907 participants from 30 states, as well as Vietnam and Canada, collectively removed 280 Burmese pythons. The competition's overall tally has now exceeded 1,600 snakes.
Tom Rahill won the $10,000 grand prize after removing 96 snakes, while Rahm Levinson received $1,000 for capturing the longest python, measuring 16 feet, five inches. Additional prizes were awarded across professional, novice and military categories.
“The number of invasive pythons removed from the Everglades during the 2026 Florida Python Challenge is a major victory for Florida’s native wildlife and a testament to what can be accomplished through strong partnerships and public participation,” FWC chairman Rodney Barreto said in a statement.
Since 2017, the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission and South Florida Water Management District contractors have removed more than 19,000 snakes. The district's robotic rabbit programme is intended to add another method to those ongoing efforts.

title: U.S. solar module production reaches historic 100 GW landmark
content:
U.S. solar module production reaches historic 100 GW landmark
The United States passed a special solar manufacturing landmark during the second quarter of 2026; cumulative domestic production of solar PV modules reached 100 GWp-dc.
While this production landmark seemed like a distant dream just a few years ago, it now serves as a sharp wake-up call to the U.S. solar industry, with domestic solar manufacturing officially shifting from optional to essential status.
The announcement here is also in stark contrast to years of hype surrounding factories that were never built, meaningless capacity metrics being added up, and a fixation on imported data.
And it is a reminder that the U.S. solar sector should stop referring to misleading third-party capacity graphs or PR-driven ‘map pins’ – and start tracking actual production numbers to see the real market.
The 100 GW number represents modules physically produced at factories in the United States, with the analysis covering more than five decades and linked directly to bottom-up company and site-level data across hundreds of factories through to today.
This research project was done in the months leading up to the inaugural Solar Manufacturing USA 2026 conference in Austin, Texas on 22-23 September 2026, forming much of the background content for the event itself, including my opening talk at the start of the first day.
Since the early 1970’s, U.S. solar PV manufacturing has gone through repeated cycles of investment, expansion, retrenchment and reinvention. Many factories were announced but never built. Others were built but operated at very low utilization rates, changed ownership or closed before producing any meaningful volume.
The 100 GW module-production crossing therefore provides a useful point to look backwards before attention turns to the next phase of the domestic U.S. solar manufacturing build-out – tracking production metrics for ingots, wafer and cells with a similar level of scrutiny from the factory-floor level.
Figure 1: Cumulative U.S. solar PV module production reached 100 GW during Q2 2026, with more than 70% added since the introduction of the Inflation Reduction Act late in 2022.
Looking back on my two-decades-plus as a solar PV market analyst, this is an article I never imagined I would write. Still less did I expect that by 2026, I would be diving deep into the factory-floor metrics of more than fifty companies across the United States—uncovering site-specific output in a furious nationwide rush to onshore an entire solar ecosystem.
Twenty years ago, during my early days at Solarbuzz, the landscape looked entirely different.Back then, my research was consumed by the entire thin-film phenomenon. I often spent my days mapping the nuances of fifteen-plus process-flow variants of CIGS panel manufacturing, an era when the U.S. was the undisputed driver of that technology.For years, U.S. solar manufacturing felt like a fascinating playground for technological learning – but not a force of global commercial significance.
My U.S. solar journey began with factory visits to the likes of Frederick and Fremont. In the intervening decades, the geographical center of manufacturing ownership radically shifted, taking me on an endless loop of flights across India, Taiwan, China, South Korea, and Southeast Asia to track the industry’s massive wave of global commoditization.
Now, the story seems to have come full-circle, and I find myself right back where I started: returning my research focus to U.S. soil, hunting down capital expenditures, process flow variants, and true production volumes at the company level.
To be the one tracking this data, at this exact moment in history, makes the announcement of this landmark milestone all the more personal and rewarding.
From global leader to industrial follower
The origins of U.S. PV manufacturing go back to the earliest commercial years of the solar industry in the 1970’s. Until 1985, the United States had produced and shipped about 100 MW of PV modules, accounting for almost all global sales over that period. At the peak, companies like Arco Solar and Solarex had annual production volumes in the mid-megawatt range – tiny numbers by today’s standards, but global solar production leadership status at the time.
During the 1990’s, Japan became the first country to build PV manufacturing plants at scale and with a supporting government/industry infrastructure that included companies with deep electronics and manufacturing experience. Linked directly to the first subsidized domestic solar end-market, this allowed Japanese PV module production to grow quickly, ultimately exceeding annual domestic U.S. production volumes by the end of the decade.
To capitalize on the growing U.S. market, these leading Japanese solar manufacturers began establishing localized module assembly plants directly within the United States. This overseas manufacturing strategy allowed them to minimize the logistical costs of shipping modules while navigating evolving local content preferences. This move ignited a broader trend, drawing a wave of foreign-owned companies eager to invest in and supply the expanding U.S. solar infrastructure.
Sharp established module manufacturing in Memphis, Tennessee, while Kyocera later assembled modules in San Diego. Sanyo invested upstream in ingot and wafer production in Salem, Oregon. However, U.S.-specific production volumes were modest compared with the manufacturing scale being created then across Asia as a whole.
This same theme was repeated with other international entrants. Chinese company Suntech opened a module factory in Arizona, while China Sunergy later established production in Sacramento.
Korean companies eventually became visible in the United States, with LG Electronics manufacturing modules in Huntsville, Alabama and Qcells (then branding/trading globally as Hanwha Q CELLS) beginning production in Dalton, Georgia.
Some of these operations lasted, but most were short-lived and of minimal long-term significance.
The thin-film boom produced more headlines than modules
The most dramatic U.S. manufacturing cycle (before the introduction of the Inflation Reduction Act at the end of 2022) came between roughly 2007 and 2012.
SolarWorld expanded its U.S. c-Si operations in Oregon, Evergreen Solar built out string ribbon production in Massachusetts, and a large group of thin-film companies attracted substantial amounts of capital.
Unisolar, Solyndra, Global Solar, MiaSole, Stion, Abound Solar and others collectively made the United States unusually thin-film-heavy during this period. The investment footprint was large, but significant production volumes failed to materialize.
Indeed, this period forms one of the most useful lessons from our 100 GW story. Capacity announcements and factory spending in the United States can dominate headlines for years without translating into sustained output.
First Solar: almost two-fifths of all U.S. production
First Solar is the major exception. Its CdTe manufacturing base in Ohio provided continuity through periods when much of the rest of U.S. module manufacturing was contracting, while recent factory builds in Alabama and Louisiana have taken domestic production volumes to significantly higher levels.
Adding up First Solar’s domestic production volumes from each of its factories in the United States, through to the end of Q2 2026, shows that approximately 39% of all solar modules ever manufactured in the United States have come from this one company.
This is an astonishing statistic—and all the more commendable given that First Solar single-handedly forged a viable thin-film alternative to the mountainous silicon-based capacity being amassed in China during this period.
Figure 2: By the end of Q2 2026, First Solar had accounted for almost 40% of all solar module production volumes accumulated since the U.S. entry into solar module manufacturing in the early 1970’s. South Korean Hanwha Solutions/Chemical’s U.S. manufacturing operations, Qcells/Q_CELLS, is the second major solar module manufacturing entity by production volumes.
Section 201 restarted c-Si; 45X changed the scale
For crystalline-silicon (c-Si) modules, the modern U.S. recovery began before the Inflation Reduction Act. U.S. c-Si production remained small and volatile through much of the 2010’s. The Section 201 safeguard period then encouraged a new group of module factories, including Qcells in Georgia and JinkoSolar in Florida, alongside LG Electronics, Silfab and Heliene.
The much larger paradigm shift arrived with the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022 and its Section 45X Advanced Manufacturing Production Credit. The lucrative 7 cents-per-watt module credit provided an immediate economic windfall for domestic assembly, while First Solar’s vertically integrated thin-film operations stood uniquely positioned to sweep up the additional, highly lucrative upstream credits available
From 2023 onward, the ranks of meaningful U.S. c-Si producers expanded rapidly. Qcells aggressively scaled its Georgia platform; T1 Energy successfully ramped its newly acquired 5 GW facility (originally built by Trina Solar) in Wilmer, Texas; and Canadian Solar established a major multi-gigawatt footprint in Mesquite.
A wave of further capacity from SEG Solar, Waaree, Illuminate, Imperial Star, JinkoSolar, Silfab, and Heliene rapidly injected volume into the market, even as First Solar pushed domestic output to historic levels with its new builds in Alabama and Louisiana
The first 100 GW – and what comes next
It took the U.S. solar industry roughly half a century to achieve its first cumulative 100 GW of module production, yet global output is now measured in hundreds of gigawatts every single year. While this disparity emphasizes how far the dominance of global manufacturing hasbshifted away from the United States, it also highlights why the domestic expansion since 2023 is fundamentally different from the smaller, volatile cycles that preceded it.
Going forward, the true test of this expansion lies entirely in factory execution: what these new facilities will actually produce, at what utilization rates, and using which technologies and supply chains. Crucially, the ultimate question is whether the wave of capital currently being deployed into domestic cells, wafers, ingots, and upstream materials can successfully coalesce into a durable, self-sustaining manufacturing ecosystem.
Given that U.S. capacity figures have lacked any real correlation to actual manufactured products since the early 2000’s, the sector must urgently move past misleading, headline-driven ‘capacity-mismatch’ metrics across the c-Si value chain. True domestic progress can only be measured by focusing on verified production metrics within an integrated ecosystem.
I will return to these critical questions in much greater detail on September 22, when I deliver the opening address at Solar Manufacturing USA 2026 in Austin, Texas.
For now, the 100 GW milestone deserves to stand on its own. It is a landmark forged over decades of U.S. solar manufacturing history – stretching from the early days of Arco Solar and Solarex, through the thin-film boom, the Section 201 restart, and the current post-IRA surge. While the next 100 GW of domestic module production is likely to materialize within just three years, long-term success will be determined by the health of the entire ecosystem, not simply module production alone.
If the silicon-based ecosystem fails to integrate as an effective, functional unit, it will simply open the door for the next major landmark in U.S. solar history: the day First Solar reaches the 100 GW milestone entirely on its own, driven purely by its independent, domestic production volumes.
